title: One nature does not mean a fixed amount of evil
source_text: Πῶς ἐκ τούτων καὶ τῶν παραπλησίων οὐ καταγέλαστος φαίνεται Κέλσος, οἰόμενος τὰ κακὰ μήτε πλείω μήτε ἥττω γενέσθαι ποτ᾿ ἄν; εἰ γὰρ καὶ μία τῶν ὅλων φύσις καὶ ἡ αὐτὴ, οὐ πάντως καὶ ἡ τῶν κακῶν γένεσις ἀεὶ ἡ αὐτή. ὡς γὰρ μιᾶς καὶ τῆς αὐτῆς οὔσης τῆς τοῦδέ τινος ἀνθρώπου φύσεως οὐκ ἀεὶ τὰ αὐτά ἐστι περὶ τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰς πράξεις, ὁτὲ μὲν οὔτε λόγον ἀνειληφότος ὁτὲ δὲ μετὰ τοῦ λόγου κακίαν, καὶ ταύτην ἤτοι ἐπὶ πλεῖον ἢ ἐπ᾿ ἔλαττον χεομένην, καὶ ἔστιν ὅτε προτραπέντος ἐπ᾿ ἀρετὴν καὶ προκόπτοντος ἐπὶ πλεῖον ἢ ἐπ᾿ ἔλαττον καὶ ἐνίοτε φθάνοντος καὶ ἐπ᾿ αὐτὴν τὴν ἀρετὴν ἐν πλείοσι θεωρίαις γινομένην ἢ ἐν ἐλάττοσιν. οὕτως ἔστιν εἰπεῖν μᾶλλον καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς τῶν ὅλων φύσεως ὅτι, εἰ καὶ μία ἐστὶ καὶ ἡ αὐτὴ τῷ γένει, ἀλλ᾿ οὐ τὰ αὐτὰ ἀεὶ οὐδ᾿ ὁμογενῆ συμβαίνει ἐν τοῖς ὅλοις· οὔτε γὰρ εὐφορίαι ἀεὶ οὔτ᾿ ἀφορίαι ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ ἐπομβρίαι οὔτε αὐχμοί· οὕτω δὲ οὐδὲ ψυχῶν κρειττόνων εὐφορίαι τεταγμέναι ἢ ἀφορίαι, καὶ χειρόνων ἐπὶ πλεῖον χύσις ἢ ἐπ᾿ ἔλαττον. καὶ ἀναγκαῖός γε τοῖς ἀκριβοῦν πάντα κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν βουλομένοις ὁ περὶ τῶν κακῶν λόγος, οὐ μενόντων ἀεὶ ἐν ταὐτῷ διὰ τὴν ἤτοι τηροῦσαν τὰ ἐπὶ γῆς πρόνοιαν ἢ κατακλυσμοῖς καὶ ἐκπυρώσεσι καθαίρουσαν, καὶ τάχα οὐ τὰ ἐπὶ γῆς μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ κόσμῳ. δεομένῳ καθαρσίου, ὅταν πολλὴ ἡ κακία γένηται ἐν αὐτῷ.
pass_a_gloss: How from these and the like (παραπλησίων) does Celsus not appear laughable (καταγέλαστος), thinking (οἰόμενος) evils could never become (γενέσθαι ποτ᾿ ἄν) more or fewer? For even if one [is] the nature of the wholes and the same, not at all (οὐ πάντως) also the coming-to-be (γένεσις) of evils always the same. For as, the nature of this particular (τοῦδέ τινος) man being one and the same, not always the same are the things about his ruling part (ἡγεμονικόν) and his reason (λόγον) and the actions (πράξεις): at one time (ὁτὲ μέν) not yet having taken up (ἀνειληφότος) reason, at another with reason vice (κακίαν), and this either poured (χεομένην) to more or to less; and there is when, having been turned (προτραπέντος) to virtue (ἀρετήν) and advancing (προκόπτοντος) to more or to less, and sometimes reaching (φθάνοντος) even to virtue itself, coming to be in more contemplations (θεωρίαις) or in fewer: so it is possible to say rather (μᾶλλον) also in the case of the nature of the wholes that, even if it is one and the same in genus (γένει), yet not always the same things nor things of same kind (ὁμογενῆ) happen (συμβαίνει) in the wholes; for neither always good harvests (εὐφορίαι) nor failures (ἀφορίαι), but neither rainy spells (ἐπομβρίαι) nor droughts (αὐχμοί); so neither of better (κρειττόνων) souls ordered (τεταγμέναι) good harvests or failures, and of worse (χειρόνων) pouring out (χύσις) to more or to less. And necessary indeed (ἀναγκαῖος) to those wishing to make everything precise (ἀκριβοῦν) as far as possible [is] the account (λόγος) about evils, not remaining always in the same (ἐν ταὐτῷ) because of the providence either keeping (τηροῦσαν) the things on earth or cleansing (καθαίρουσαν) [them] with floods (κατακλυσμοῖς) and conflagrations (ἐκπυρώσεσι), and perhaps not the things on earth only but also those in the whole world (κόσμῳ), needing a cleansing (καθαρσίου) whenever much vice comes to be in it.
pass_b_english: From these things and others like them, how can Celsus fail to look ridiculous when he thinks that evils could never become more or fewer? For even if the nature of the whole is one and the same, it does not at all follow that the origin of evils too is always the same.

For take a particular man. His nature is one and the same, yet things are not always the same with his ruling part, his reason and his actions. At one time he has not yet taken on reason; at another he has taken on vice along with reason, and this vice spreads further or less far. And there are times when he has been turned toward virtue and advances further or less far; and sometimes he even reaches virtue itself, which is found in more contemplations or in fewer.

So it is possible to say all the more of the nature of the whole that, even if it is one and the same in kind, the same things, or things of the same kind, do not always happen in the whole. For there are not always good harvests, nor always failed ones, nor always heavy rains, nor always droughts. So, too, the plenty or the dearth of better souls is not fixed, nor is the spread of worse souls, further or less far.

Indeed, for those who wish to examine everything as precisely as they can, the account of evils is necessary: evils do not always remain in the same state, because of providence, which either preserves what is on earth or cleanses it with floods and conflagrations; and perhaps not only what is on earth but also what is in the whole world, which needs cleansing whenever vice grows great in it.

choices.choice: restored καὶ ('the origin of evils too') and γάρ ('For take a particular man')

last paragraph: the account of evils and the clause 'not remaining always the same' rejoined with a colon (had been split into an unconnected new sentence); 'an account' -> 'the account'; ἀναγκαῖός γε -> 'Indeed ... necessary'
ὅταν: 'once vice has grown great' -> 'whenever vice grows great'; removed doubled 'when ... once'

'Reaches virtue itself, which is found in more contemplations or in fewer': γινομένην agrees with ἀρετήν, so the 'more or fewer contemplations' belong to virtue, not to the man; kept so. 'Has not yet taken on reason' (οὔτε λόγον ἀνειληφότος): the stage before reason is acquired, as the following 'at another ... along with reason' shows; 'yet' makes that sequence plain. 'Floods and conflagrations' echoes Plato's Timaeus (cited in 4.62) and the Stoic conflagration; no Scripture is quoted, and the Flood of Genesis is not named, so no citation added. Koetschau's full stop before δεομένῳ καθαρσίου is treated as a light pause: the dative agrees with κόσμῳ ('the whole world, which needs cleansing'). The genitive absolute οὐ μενόντων ἀεὶ ἐν ταὐτῷ gives the content of 'the account of evils' and is joined to it with a colon. 'Origin' renders γένεσις as in 4.62 and 4.65-66.
